verdicts.review_was_substantively_correct: All seven named items were reproduced in source. Items 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 required code or contract changes; item 4 was a false contract with no UB, corrected as such. The ownership/release model itself (RawCtx/OwnedCtx/OwnedBlock transitions) was not contradicted and was not changed.
verdicts.alignment_note: The defect is real even though every current implementor is pointer-aligned: `OwnedCtx::zalloc` and `RawCtx::malloc` are safe fns, and a conforming CtxDestroy implementor with `#[repr(align(64))]` received `NonNull<Self>` built over a merely pointer-aligned `CRYPTO_malloc` block. `size_of::<T>()` and the allocation were otherwise authority-exact, which is exactly why the alignment obligation was hidden.

items.class: soundness: misaligned NonNull<T> through a safe constructor
items.change: Added `crate::runtime::mem::SEAM_MALLOC_ALIGN` (the alignment the seam guarantees) and refuse, with the allocation-refusal arm (`None`), any type whose `align_of::<T>()` exceeds it: `RawCtx::malloc_at`/`zalloc_at` (and therefore `OwnedCtx::zalloc`/`zalloc_at`), and `asn1::owned::OwnedBlock::malloc`/`zalloc`. `OwnedCtx::from_raw_at` and `OwnedBlock::from_raw` additionally refuse a non-NULL misaligned pointer instead of constructing an owner that would dereference it. The `CtxDestroy` contract now states that over-aligned implementors are refused by the constructors, so the alignment gap is not a hidden implementor obligation.
items.why_this_bound: `CRYPTO_malloc`'s default branch is libc `malloc` and an installed branch must be malloc-compatible, but neither the OpenSSL interface nor this crate's seam contract promises more than fundamental-type alignment. The conservative, always-conforming bound used is `align_of::<*mut c_void>()` (pointer alignment). `max_align_t` would admit more types, but only by assuming a C-library detail that a caller-installed hook is not contractually required to honour.
items.accepted_limitation: A type aligned above pointer alignment is refused even where libc malloc would in fact align it. The result is a refused allocation (authority failure semantics), never a misaligned owner. No current CtxDestroy implementor or OwnedBlock<T> instantiation is affected (all are align <= pointer alignment).

items.class: wrong contract: ASN1_mbstring_ncopy/copy did not require a usable *out
items.outcome: FIXED (contract; the authority-shaped reuse is retained)
items.change: Both functions now state the real precondition: `*out`, when non-NULL, is a live, exclusively owned `ASN1_STRING` whose `data` is NULL or a live seam allocation no other owner holds and that `in` does not alias (the function releases it with `ASN1_STRING_set0(dest, NULL, 0)`); `len >= -1`; BMP/UNIV multiples; `len < INT_MAX`; `inform` one of the four forms. `in` must not alias the released data. No runtime change: C callers legitimately pass their own object to be overwritten, so making the slot null-only would break the authority interface.
